title: GNU tar
summary: GNU tar archives trees. It is not coreutils and not cp. Sparse files, --exclude, listings, and reproducible metadata are tar's own flags.
text:
GNU tar reads and writes tape archives. It is not GNU coreutils. Ubuntu package `tar`, upstream GNU tar 1.35. `cp -a` copies a tree and keeps it as a tree. tar packs members into one file with its own headers. Checksums of a tree and checksums of a tarball answer different questions. Compression is a second program, gzip or zstd or the others in the next lesson, even when tar has a `-z` or `-I` switch that calls them. This lesson stays with the archive itself so the format is visible.

`tar -cf bundle.tar members` creates. `tar -tf bundle.tar` lists names. `tar -xf bundle.tar` extracts into the current directory. List before you extract. An archive can contain absolute paths or `..` members; GNU tar's defaults are safer than the oldest tar, and you should still look at `-t` before `-x` on an archive you did not write. Extract into a fresh directory when you are not sure.

`--exclude=drop.txt` skips a member while creating. Patterns are tar's, not the shell's, once they are quoted. Exclude build outputs, `.git`, and device files you do not want in a source drop. `--exclude` does not reach inside an archive you are only listing. It filters what gets added.

Sparse files are the disk feature `truncate` and `cp --sparse` already use in the coreutils lessons. A hole has a large apparent size and a small allocated size. `tar --sparse` records the hole. Without it, tar reads the zeros and stores them, and the archive grows to the apparent size plus headers. `wc -c` on the two archives is the proof. `du` and `stat` on the original file are the coreutils view of the same hole. The companion benchmark `sparse-tar` repeats that comparison on an 8 MiB hole and records both the medians and the archive sizes. Those sizes are measurements from that run. The example in this lesson prints `wc -c` for a 1 MiB hole so you can see the same mechanism on a fixture. Do not add the two experiments together.

Reproducible tarballs need fixed metadata. Default tar stores your user name, the file's mtime, and directory order that can follow readdir. Two creates of the same bytes then hash differently. `--sort=name` fixes the member order. `--owner=0 --group=0 --numeric-owner` stores numeric ids instead of the capture host's account. `--mtime=@0` stores the epoch. `cmp` of two archives built that way succeeds. `sha256sum` then names those bytes. GNU gzip's `-n` is the matching idea for the compressed wrapper, and it belongs to the compression lesson. This lesson's reproducible archive is uncompressed so the hash is tar's.

`--mtime` and `--owner` do not change the file on disk. They change the header in the archive. Extracting that archive as yourself creates files owned by you, unless you are root, which these scripts refuse to be.

For a backup you intend to restore once, a fast compressor with threads (pigz, `zstd -T`) is usually the right wrapper. For a release artifact you will download a million times, a slower higher ratio can win, and that choice is the next lesson's benchmark, not a property of tar.

title: gzip, pigz, bzip2, xz, and zstd
summary: Five compressors, five upstreams, none of them coreutils. pigz and zstd -T spend cores. Levels trade CPU for bytes. The companion benchmark records both on a repetitive log and on random bytes.
text:
Compression is not coreutils. `gzip` is GNU gzip, Ubuntu package `gzip`. `pigz` is pigz by Mark Adler, Ubuntu package `pigz`, and it writes the same format as gzip using several threads. `bzip2` is the bzip2 package, upstream bzip2. `xz` is XZ Utils, Ubuntu package `xz-utils`. `zstd` is Zstandard, Ubuntu package `zstd`, upstream Facebook's zstd. They differ in format. A file gzip wrote is not a file zstd can read. Round-trip with the same tool, and check the bytes with `cmp`, which is diffutils, or with `sha256sum`, which is coreutils.

`gzip -n` omits the original name and timestamp from the header. Two runs then produce the same bytes. Without `-n`, the header carries the clock and the hash changes. Release artifacts and any test that compares compressed bytes want `-n`. pigz accepts `-n` for the same reason. zstd and xz have their own headers. Do not assume `-n` is universal.

Levels buy ratio with CPU and sometimes with memory. gzip's `-1` is fast and larger, `-9` is slower and smaller, `-6` is a common default. zstd's negative and low levels are very fast, the middle levels are the usual default range, and levels past 19 require `--ultra` and more memory. This course does not time `--ultra`. xz's high levels are slow and memory-hungry. bzip2's block sorting is often the slow choice on both repetitive logs and random bytes, and sometimes still smaller. "Often" is not a number. The benchmark is the number.

Threads are a second axis. `pigz -p 1` uses one worker. `pigz -p 4` uses four. The format stays gzip, so a normal gzip can decompress it. `zstd -T1` is one thread. `zstd -T4` asks for four. `zstd -T0` means one thread per detected core, which changes meaning when you move the script from a laptop to a 64-core builder. Prefer an explicit count in a script. Stacking GNU parallel `-j 4` around `zstd -T4` multiplies the cores. Pick one pool.

The harness in `benchmarks/measure_companions.py` compressed 1 MiB two ways. `compress-compressible` is a repeated log line. `compress-random` is bytes from a seeded PRNG, which will not collapse. Each variant ran five times. The note records the compressed sizes from one extra pass using the same flags. Read both benches. A tool that looks wonderful on the log can tie the others on the random file, because there is no ratio left to win and only the CPU tax remains. Medians include the Python starter. The page cache was warm. Nothing was tuned. The performance section quotes the medians from that file.

Decompression is usually cheaper than compression and is single-threaded in several of these tools even when compression was threaded. A backup you restore often should be timed on the decode, not only on the encode. This course's timed trials are encodes to stdout, discarded by the harness. The lesson examples decode and `cmp` so the round trip is proven on a tiny file. That tiny file is not the benchmark.

title: GNU time and hyperfine
summary: The bash keyword time is not GNU time. /usr/bin/time -v reports RSS and faults. hyperfine repeats a command. Neither tool is coreutils, and a sub-millisecond sample is not a ranking.
text:
There are two commands named time, and only one of them is a program. Bash has a keyword `time`. `type time` prints `time is a shell keyword`. The keyword times a pipeline in the shell's own way and prints `real`, `user`, and `sys`. It does not accept GNU time's `-f` or `-v`. If you write `time -f %x true`, bash tries to execute a command named `-f` and reports `command not found`. It may still print a timing line afterward. That combination is the usual reason a copied snippet "almost" works.

`/usr/bin/time` is the Ubuntu package `time`, upstream GNU time. The package version on this host is 1.9. The binary's own version string says `UNKNOWN`, which is a packaging quirk, not a reason to ignore `dpkg -S`. GNU time's `-f` takes a format. `%x` is the child's exit status. `%e` is elapsed wall time. `%M` is maximum resident set size in kilobytes. `-v` prints a long list: user time, system time, percent CPU, elapsed time, maximum RSS, page faults, context switches, and more. Those fields are why you wanted the binary. The keyword does not print maximum RSS.

The `-v` values for `/usr/bin/true` are tiny and noisy. A single capture would put a page-fault count and a CPU percent on the page that the next run would not repeat. The example strips everything after the last colon so you can see the field names and not a fake measurement. When you need numbers, use the harness. It runs five trials, takes the median, records user, system, and `ru_maxrss`, and writes `public/benchmarks/companions.json` with the CPU model, the memory total, and the tool versions. The Python process that starts the command is included in the elapsed time. Compare variants with each other. Do not treat the absolute seconds as a shell-only figure, and do not compare them with `sample-run.json` or `supplements.json`. Those files are other runs.

hyperfine is the Ubuntu package `hyperfine`, upstream sharkdp/hyperfine, version 1.18.0 here. It warms up, repeats, and reports a mean and a spread. `--shell=none` executes the argv directly so the shell is not inside the number. Commands that finish in a few hundred microseconds trigger its warning that the result is inside calibration noise. `/usr/bin/true` is such a command. The example runs hyperfine and then replaces digit runs with `N`, so the shape of the report and the warning are visible and the microseconds are not quoted as a result. Use hyperfine when you are comparing two commands that run long enough for the warning to stay quiet. Use the course harness when the result has to sit in the benchmark file next to a disclosure.

Neither tool is coreutils. Coreutils `date` can difference two timestamps and is the wrong profiler. `timeout` bounds a hung command and does not report RSS.

Wall time, user time, and system time answer different questions. Wall time includes waiting. User time is CPU in the process. System time is CPU in the kernel on its behalf. A grep that looks slow on the wall and idle in user time is waiting on a pipe or a disk. A gzip that burns user time is CPU bound. Maximum RSS tells you whether the process grew. GNU time's `-v` is one sample of all of those. The harness median is the sample this course is willing to keep.

hyperfine's mean is not the harness median. Do not average them. Do not paste a hyperfine table for `/usr/bin/true` into a slide. The warning in the captured shape is the tool telling you the command was too short.

title: strace, ltrace, and perf
summary: strace sees system calls. ltrace sees library calls. perf would see hardware counters and is not installed for this kernel. None of them are coreutils.
text:
strace traces system calls. It is not coreutils. Ubuntu package `strace`, upstream strace, version 6.8 here. A system call is the boundary between the process and the kernel: `write`, `read`, `openat`, `execve`, `clone`. When a pipeline is slow or a program fails with a surprising `ENOENT`, strace shows the calls and the errors. It does not show which C++ function burned the CPU. That is a profiler question.

`-e trace=write` keeps one family of calls so the log is readable. `-o` writes the trace to a file instead of mixing it with the program's stderr. Addresses and file-descriptor details are in that log. The example rewrites hex addresses to `ADDR` and the return count's trailing integer so the capture shows `write(1, "hello\n", 6)` without a number that changes. `-c` prints a summary table: calls, errors, and time per syscall. The times in that table are a single run's accounting. They are useful at the terminal and they are the wrong thing to freeze into a lesson as a ranking. The example checks that the summary mentions `write` and prints a stable line.

`-f` follows children. A shell pipeline is several processes. Without `-f` you see the shell and miss `grep`. With `-f` you see each child's calls, tagged with a pid. Pids change every run, so the example filters to the `write` lines and strips addresses. You are looking for the call, not the pid.

ltrace traces dynamic library calls. Ubuntu package `ltrace`, version 0.7.3. It is the view one level above strace. `/usr/bin/echo` ends in `write` at the syscall layer and in `fputs_unlocked` at the libc layer. ltrace's raw lines contain load addresses. ASLR changes them every execution. The example keeps only the function names, sorted and unique. That list is the teaching artifact. ltrace misses statically linked calls and it can miss functions the compiler inlined. A quiet ltrace is not proof that nothing ran.

perf is the Linux performance-counter tool, upstream the kernel's `tools/perf`, documented in `perf-stat(1)` and on the kernel wiki. The method, which this host cannot execute, is `perf stat -e cycles,instructions -- command` for a count, and `perf record -g -- command` followed by `perf report` for a sample of call stacks. Those commands need a `perf` binary built for the running kernel. Ubuntu 24.04's `linux-tools` packages in the archive track kernel 6.8. This host runs 6.12.113+. There is no matching package to install, and a mismatched binary is not a measurement. The example prints `perf-absent`. No cycle count appears anywhere in this course.

strace and ltrace slow the target. They add context switches on every call. A `-c` summary of a program that was traced is not the speed of the untraced program. Use them to see what happened. Use the harness, GNU time, or hyperfine to see how long an untraced command took. Do not leave a strace attached to a production process to "just look". The overhead is the look.

Tracing answers "which call", not "how fast would it have been". The cost is roughly proportional to the number of calls. A `write` of one byte in a loop becomes a different program under strace. `-e` limits the tax and the log. `-c` avoids storing every line and still perturbs time. For a pipeline, start with `strace -c -f` at the terminal, read the busiest calls, then drop the tracer and time the untraced command with the harness.

I/O wait shows up as time in `read` and `write` that does not match user CPU from GNU time. CPU-bound compression shows up as user time with few syscalls. That pairing is the method. This lesson's examples are `echo`, which is too small to time. The compression and grep benches are the untraced numbers.

ltrace is heavier and less complete than strace on modern binaries. Prefer strace when the question is the kernel. Prefer a real profil

title: pv, iostat, vmstat, and pidstat
summary: pv measures a pipe. iostat and pidstat are sysstat. vmstat is procps, not sysstat. None of them are coreutils. Live counters are not copied into the prose.
text:
These four tools tell you where time went. None of them are GNU coreutils. `pv` is Pipe Viewer, Ubuntu package `pv`, upstream the ivarch program. It copies standard input to standard output and writes progress on standard error. `iostat` and `pidstat` are the Ubuntu package `sysstat`, upstream sysstat. `vmstat` looks similar and is not in that package. On this image `/usr/bin/vmstat` is `procps`, upstream procps-ng, the same family as `ps` and `free`. Filing vmstat under sysstat is the mistake this lesson exists to prevent.

`pv` is how you see the rate of a pipe. `tar -c dir | pv | zstd` shows bytes moving between tar and zstd. The progress is on stderr so it does not enter the archive. `-b` asks for a byte count. `-F` sets the format. `-q` copies with no progress, which is the right flag when you only wanted the splice and a later `cmp`. A progress bar uses carriage returns. The example uses `-F '%b'` so the capture is a single size for a 7-byte input. That size is the input's size, not a throughput ranking.

`iostat` reports CPU and device counters since boot, and then a sample if you pass an interval and a count. `iostat -c 1 1` is one CPU sample. The header names `%user`, `%nice`, `%system`, `%iowait`, `%steal`, and `%idle`. `%iowait` is time the CPU was idle and at least one process wanted disk. It is not "disk percent" by itself. `%steal` is time a hypervisor took. The numbers move every second. The example prints the header only.

`vmstat 1` prints a header and then lines of runnable processes, memory, swap, blocks in and out, interrupts, context switches, and CPU states. Two samples are the minimum if you want a rate, because the first line is an average since boot and the later lines are the interval. The example prints the two header rows, which do not contain a sample. `bi` and `bo` are blocks in and out. `wa` is I/O wait. `id` is idle. A backup that is disk bound shows up in `bi`/`bo` and `wa`, not in a high `%user`.

`pidstat` is per process. It can show CPU, and with `-d` disk, for tasks it can see. The header includes `%CPU` and `Command`. The first column of a data row is a clock. Clocks change, so the example rewrites the header line to start at `UID` and drops the average row. You learn the columns. You do not freeze this host's idle percentage into the paragraph.

Coreutils `dd` can report a byte count and a time with `status=progress`. That report is dd's own. pv is the tool when the program in the middle of the pipe has no progress flag. Neither one is a disk profiler. iostat is closer, and it still needs a sample window you chose, not a single boot-average line.

## Performance

A pipe's throughput is the minimum of the producer, the consumer, and the copy in between. pv sits in the middle and is an extra copy. On a fast zstd of a cached file, pv can become visible. On a disk-bound tar of a cold tree, pv is noise and iostat's `%iowait` and block counters are the signal. Measure the unadorned pipeline with the harness when you want a median. Insert pv when you want to see which stage is stalled. Remove it before you record the number.

`iostat` and `vmstat` without an interval print a long average. A machine that was idle all morning and busy for ten seconds still looks idle in the since-boot line. Pass an interval. title: ps, top, free, pgrep, and pkill
summary: ps, top, free, pgrep, and pkill are procps, upstream procps-ng. They are not coreutils. pkill matches a name, and a careless pattern matches your shell.
text:
`ps`, `top`, `free`, `pgrep`, and `pkill` are the Ubuntu package `procps`, upstream procps-ng. They are not GNU coreutils. The GNU coreutils manual documents a `kill` and an `uptime` that Ubuntu ships from this same procps package, which is why those names feel like coreutils and are not. `pgrep` selects processes. `pkill` sends them a signal. Default signal is TERM. `ps` is a snapshot. `top` repeats a snapshot. `free` reads the kernel's memory totals.

`ps -o comm= -p $$` prints the command name of the current shell, which is `bash` in these scripts. `comm` is the short name, not the full argument list. `args` is the full list and will contain your script text. That difference matters the moment you search.

`free -b` prints totals in bytes. The columns are total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available. `available` is the estimate of memory a new program can have without swapping. `free` alone is not that estimate, because caches are reclaimable. The example prints the header and the row labels `Mem:` and `Swap:` and drops the integers. The integers are a live sample. They are not a benchmark of your C++ allocator. RSS of one process is GNU time's `%M` or `ps -o rss=`, not the machine total.

`top -b -n 1` is one batch frame, safe in a script. Without `-b`, top takes the terminal. The PID header lists the columns: PID, USER, PR, NI, VIRT, RES, SHR, S, %CPU, %MEM, TIME+, COMMAND. `%CPU` in one frame is a short sample and it lies for a process that started a moment ago. The example prints that header only.

`pgrep -x` matches the exact comm name. A pattern without `-x` is a regular expression against the name, and `-f` matches the full argument list. `-f` is how a script kills itself: the pattern appears in the shell's argv, `pgrep -f` sees the shell, `pkill -f` signals the shell. The safe demo copies `/usr/bin/sleep` to a file named `cuwbnap` and matches `-x cuwbnap`. The shell's comm stays `bash`. The script text never needs to be the pattern that `-f` would scan. Start it, check that `pgrep -x` finds it, `pkill -x` it, and check that it is gone. `pgrep` exits 1 when nothing matches. An `if` absorbs that status. `wait` on a killed sleep returns non-zero. `wait || true` records the child without failing the script.

Do not point `pkill` at `sleep`, `java`, `python`, or `bash` on a shared machine. Those names are other people's processes. A unique comm, or a pid you just printed from a child you spawned, is the whole safety story.

`ps` and `top` can see more processes than your user, depending on hidepid mounts. They cannot see inside another user's address space. `lsof` is the next lesson when the question is "who holds this file".

## Performance

`ps` and `pgrep` read the process table. On a quiet machine they are cheap. On a host with a huge number of tasks they are still metadata, not a profiler. Running `ps` in a loop to watch a build is how you spend a core printing. `pidstat 1` from sysstat is the sampler built for that, and it is not procps. `top -d 5` is a coarse repeat. None of these replace a median from the harness.

`free` is a single read of kernel counters. It does not show which process to blame. A process with a large RSS shows up in `ps -o rss`. The companion harness records `ru_maxrss` of the children it waited for, which is the peak of those children, not the machine total from `free`. Do not add them.

`pkill` is not a performance tool. A script that restarts a worker by killing a name pays the process startup the startup benchmark already measured for `/usr/bin/true`. Killing and respawning a compiler to "free memory" is that cost plus lost caches. Measure the leak before you automate the kill.

title: lsof and fuser
summary: lsof lists open descriptors. fuser names the processes that hold a path. lsof is the lsof package. fuser is psmisc. Neither is coreutils. A deleted path can stay open.
text:
`lsof` lists open files. It is not GNU coreutils. Ubuntu package `lsof`, upstream lsof. A "file" here is a descriptor: a regular file, a directory, a socket, a pipe. `fuser` answers a narrower question: which processes have this path open. Ubuntu package `psmisc`, upstream psmisc. It is not procps and not coreutils. Exit status 1 from `fuser` means no process held the path. Exit status 0 means at least one did. The table goes to stderr. Pids go to stdout. Both move, so the examples search for a stable word instead of printing the pid.

The Android and server case you actually hit is a log that was rotated or removed while a process still has it open. `rm` unlinks the directory entry. The inode remains until the last descriptor closes. `df` still shows the blocks. `ls` does not show the name. `lsof` shows the descriptor and marks it `(deleted)`. The example opens `hold.txt` on descriptor 3, removes the name, and looks for that marker. The path in the raw lsof line includes the scratch directory, which changes every capture, so the check is the marker and the basename, not the absolute path.

`lsof -a -p $$ -d 3` combines filters with AND. Without `-a`, extra selectors sometimes widen the search. `-Fn` is a parseable field mode. The `n` field is the name. Stripping directories leaves `hold.txt`, which is stable. This shell is the process. You do not need to lsof the whole machine to learn the tool, and a whole-machine lsof is slow and full of other users' sockets you should not publish.

`fuser -v hold.txt` while descriptor 3 is open reports this bash. Without `-v`, fuser prints a pid and not the command name. The example greps stderr for `bash` and prints `fuser-sees-bash`. A file nobody has open is the opposite case. `fuser` returns 1. The example records `fuser_closed:1`. Do not use `fuser -k`. That flag sends a signal, which is `pkill`'s job with a name you chose, not a sweep of whoever has a directory open. Killing every process that has a build tree open will kill your editor.

Permissions apply. lsof shows what you are allowed to see. Another user's descriptors may be hidden. A failure to see a pid is not proof the pid is gone.

Coreutils `ls` and `stat` look at directory entries. They do not list descriptors. That is why a deleted open file confuses `du` and `df`: `du` walks names, `df` sees blocks. lsof is the missing list.

`lsof` without a pid walks every descriptor it can open in `/proc`. On a busy host that is a lot of reads of small files, and it is slow. Always pass `-p` when you know the process. `-d` limits the descriptor. The examples do both. A cron job that runs unrestricted `lsof` every second will show up in its own `pidstat` as a CPU and metadata cost.

`fuser` on a single path is a smaller walk. `fuser` on a directory can match every process using any file under it, depending on flags, and that list is large. Ask for the file.

Neither tool changes I/O throughput. They explain a `du`/`df` disagreement after a delete. The fix for the space is to close the descriptor or restart the holder, not to run lsof again. Restarting is process startup, which the coreutils startup supplement measured for a trivial binary. A fat JVM is more.

These examples do not print byte rates. There is no companion-benchmark row for lsof, because a correct lsof of one descriptor is noise next to the harness.

title: The util-linux toolbox
summary: column, rev, flock, taskset, ionice, fallocate, findmnt, lsblk, script, logger, setsid, and prlimit come from util-linux. Ubuntu splits that source into util-linux, bsdutils, and bsdextrautils. None of them are coreutils.
text:
util-linux is an upstream project, not a single Ubuntu binary package, and it is not GNU coreutils. `dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}'` on `bsdutils` and `bsdextrautils` prints `util-linux`. The binaries are split. `column` is `bsdextrautils`. `script` and `logger` are `bsdutils`. `rev`, `flock`, `taskset`, `ionice`, `fallocate`, `findmnt`, `lsblk`, `setsid`, and `prlimit` are the `util-linux` binary package. Learn the binary package, because that is what `dpkg -S` prints and what an install line needs. Learn the source, because that is where the manual and the bugs live.

`column -t` aligns whitespace-separated fields into a table. It is a presentation tool. It does not parse CSV quotes. `rev` reverses each line. Both are byte tools with locale edges. They are the right hammer for a quick look at `ps` output and the wrong hammer for a file format.

`flock` takes an advisory lock on a file and runs a command. Two backup scripts can share one lock file so they do not run at once. `-n` fails immediately if the lock is held, which is what a cron job wants. The example holds the lock in a background `sleep` and shows the second `flock -n` failing. Advisory means a program that never calls flock is not stopped. It is a contract, not a kernel denial of writes.

`taskset -c 0` pins a process to CPU 0. The shell expands `$$` before `taskset` starts, so `taskset -c -p $$` reports the shell, not the child. Run the query inside the child: `taskset -c 0 bash -c 'taskset -c -p $$'`. The affinity list is then `0`. The benchmark id `taskset-pin` times `sha256sum` of 8 MiB with and without that pin. Read the note. A single-threaded checksum often does not separate. The pin is still real, and the example proves the affinity. No frequency scaling was changed. `taskset` is not a performance boost by itself.

`ionice -c 3` asks for the idle I/O class. The child in the example prints `idle`. The class is a hint to the kernel scheduler. It is not a bandwidth cap in bytes per second. On a quiet disk you will not see a difference. On a disk a backup is saturating, idle I/O waits. This course does not saturate a disk and does not time ionice.

`fallocate -l` reserves blocks. `fallocate --punch-hole` releases them in the middle of a file and leaves the apparent size from `stat` unchanged. `du` reports allocated bytes and drops. That is the same hole story as `truncate`, done through the fallocate system call. Filesystems differ. This host's ext4 accepted the punch. A filesystem that does not will return an error, and the script should notice.

`findmnt -n -o FSTYPE /` prints the root filesystem type. `df -T` from coreutils is the space view. They should agree on the type name. `lsblk` lists block devices. Names like `vda` are this machine's. The example prints only the unique `TYPE` values so a disk rename does not rewrite the lesson. Do not script against a device node you saw here.

`script` records a typescript of a command. The file contains a header with a timestamp and a carriage return after the payload. Strip `\r` before you grep for an exact line. `logger` writes to syslog. `--no-act` still opens `/dev/log` on this version, and this host has no such socket, so the status is failure. The example prints that status and the error. It does not claim a log line was stored. `setsid` starts a new session. Compare session ids of the parent and of a `setsid bash -c 'ps -o sid= -p $$'` child. They differ. `prlimit --nofile=64` runs a child whose `ulimit -n` is 64. `ulimit` is the shell builtin. `prlimit` is the program that can set the limit on a command without changing the rest of the script.

title: bc, jq, ripgrep, fd, moreutils, and entr
summary: Small tools that show up in real scripts and are still not coreutils. bc does arithmetic, jq reads JSON, rg and fdfind search, moreutils patches shell gaps, and entr reruns a command.
text:
These helpers sit next to shell scripts. None of them are GNU coreutils.

`bc` is GNU bc, Ubuntu package `bc` 1.07.1. It is arbitrary-precision arithmetic. `scale=2; 1/3` prints `.33` with no leading zero. That missing zero breaks a later tool that expects `0.33`. `printf` from coreutils can format a number bc already computed, or you can ask bc to print a leading zero yourself. The shell's `$((1/3))` is integer arithmetic and is the wrong tool when the fraction matters. bc is the right tool, and it is still a program you start, so do not call it once per line of a million-line file. One awk process adds a column faster. bc is for the expression you do not want to get wrong.

`jq` is jq, Ubuntu package `jq`, upstream jqlang. It filters JSON. It is not a streaming editor for random logs. A saved API response is a file. This course's sandboxes have no network and must not grow one, so the example writes the JSON in the script and treats it as a fixture you might have saved from an API. `jq -r '.items[].name'` prints raw strings. Pipe them to `sort` when you need order. jq's own `sort` exists and is a different language. Use it when you are already in jq. Use coreutils `sort` when the next step is a coreutils pipeline.

ripgrep is `/usr/bin/rg`, Ubuntu package `ripgrep`, upstream BurntSushi ripgrep. It is not GNU grep. Inside a git work tree it skips files ignored by `.gitignore`. The example builds a tiny tree with a `.git` directory and a `.gitignore` that hides `skip.log`, then shows that `rg` prints `keep me` and hides `secret` until `--no-ignore`. That default is why people love it in a Rust or Android tree full of build output, and it is why a script that must see the ignored file has to say `--no-ignore` or call `/usr/bin/grep`. A binary named `rg` earlier on `PATH` may be a different build. The examples call `/usr/bin/rg`.

`fd` is the upstream name. Ubuntu's package `fd-find` installs `/usr/bin/fdfind`, which is a symlink to the fd binary. There is no `/usr/bin/fd` on this image. `fdfind -t f` lists files. It is not findutils. It respects ignore rules in a project and it is faster to type. A script that must be POSIX and complete should still call `find -print0`. Use fdfind for interactive search and for project trees where the ignore rules are the point.

moreutils is Ubuntu package `moreutils`, upstream Joey Hess's moreutils. `sponge` reads all of stdin, then writes the file. `sort file | sponge file` is the way to sort a file onto itself. A redirection `sort file > file` truncates the file before sort reads it. `ts` prefixes a timestamp. The clock changes, so the example checks the shape and prints `ts-prefixed` instead of the time. `ifne` runs a command only when stdin is non-empty, which keeps a watcher from firing on an empty grep. `chronic` hides the output of a successful command and shows it when the command fails, which is what you want from a cron job that is quiet until it breaks. moreutils also had a `parallel`. GNU parallel diverted it to `parallel.moreutils`. Do not confuse the two.

`entr` watches files and runs a command. Ubuntu package `entr`, upstream eradman entr. `-n` avoids touching the terminal. `-z` exits after the utility finishes. The example feeds one file name and prints `ran-once`. A long-running watch is a development loop, not a capture. The manual on the project site describes the file list on stdin.

It is not a sandbox by itself. This course prints the package and the version line and does not call chroot on a directory. Status 125 means chroot itself failed; 126 and 127 mean the inner command could not be started.

title: cksum
summary: Print or verify checksums.
text: The historical CRC plus byte count is still the default. -a selects md5, the SHA-2 family, blake2b, sm3, and the old sum algorithms. --tag is how cryptographic digests print a BSD-style line; the CRC line stays numeric.

title: comm
summary: Compare sorted files FILE1 and FILE2 line by line.
text: Compares two sorted files line by line and prints three columns. GNU comm checks order and exits 1 when it is wrong, after it may already have written lines. Suppress columns with -1, -2, and -3.

title: cp
summary: Copy SOURCE to DEST, or multiple SOURCE(s) to DIRECTORY.
text: Copies files and trees. -a is -dR --preserve=all. --reflink=always fails on this ext4 filesystem; --reflink=auto falls back to a read/write copy. --sparse controls holes. -n is marked non-portable in 9.4; use --update=none.

title: csplit
summary: Output pieces of FILE separated by PATTERN(s) to files 'xx00', 'xx01', ...,
text: Splits a file at context lines rather than at a fixed size. Patterns are basic regular expressions. -z suppresses empty pieces. It is not a CSV or JSON parser. Stock macOS does not ship GNU csplit.

title: cut
summary: Print selected parts of lines from each FILE to standard output.
text: Selects byte, character, or field ranges. -d sets a single-byte delimiter. It does not understand quotes, so a CSV comma inside quotes is still a separator. --complement and --output-delimiter are GNU extensions.

title: date
summary: Display date and time in the given FORMAT.
text: Formats and parses dates. -d takes a date string, including @epoch. BSD date uses -v and -f instead. --debug explains a parse. The clock resolution reported by --resolution is a property of this host.

title: dd
summary: Copy a file, converting and formatting according to the operands.
text: Copies blocks. status=progress and status=none are GNU. conv=sparse seeks over NUL blocks. iflag=fullblock matters when reading a pipe that returns short reads. Never point of= at a device in an example you have not identified.

title: df
summary: Show information about the file system on which each FILE resides,
text: Reports filesystem free space from statfs, not by walking files. GNU df -T prints the type. On BSD, df -T filters by type instead. --output and -T cannot be combined. This host's df -T says ext4 where stat -f says ext2/ext3.

title: dir
summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
text: dir is ls with a different default format, still the same coreutils binary family. Scripts should call ls with explicit options so a dir default never becomes part of the contract.

title: dircolors
summary: Output commands to set the LS_COLORS environment variable.
text: Prints shell commands that set LS_COLORS. The database is not consulted unless the shell evaluates that output. Color is a display hint. It does not change the bytes ls writes when --color=never.

title: dirname
summary: Output each NAME with its last non-slash component and trailing slashes
text: Prints everything through the last slash. Multiple operands are allowed. -z changes the output delimiter; it does not make dirname read NUL-separated stdin. A path with no slash yields '.'.

title: du
summary: Summarize device usage of the set of FILEs, recursively for directories.
text: Walks a tree and sums allocated space, counting a hard link once unless -l is set. --apparent-size or -b reports the logical size, which is what sparse files make diverge from du without that flag. df does not walk the tree.

title: echo
summary: Echo the STRING(s) to standard output.
text: The manual recommends printf for anything that must be portable. Bash's builtin echo ignores --help and prints the word. /usr/bin/echo is coreutils, and -E (no escapes) is its default. -e is a GNU behavior, not POSIX.

title: env
summary: Set each NAME to VALUE in the environment and run COMMAND.
text: Runs a command with a modified environment. -i starts empty, -u removes a name, -C changes directory, and -S splits a string for shebangs. The manual lists env among commands with special exit statuses. BSD env lacks -S.

title: expand
summary: Convert tabs in each FILE to spaces, writing to standard output.
text: Turns tabs into spaces. -t sets tab stops. -i affects only leading tabs. It does not reflow paragraphs; fmt does that. Tabs inside the data are bytes, not a table layout.

title: expr
summary: Print the value of EXPRESSION to standard output.  A blank line below
text: Evaluates an expression and prints it. A true comparison prints 1 and exits 0. A false comparison prints 0 and exits 1. That inversion surprises people who treat the printed number as the exit status. Prefer test or shell arithmetic for new scripts.

title: factor
summary: Print the prime factors of each specified integer NUMBER.  If none
text: Prints prime factors of arbitrary-precision integers. factor 1 and factor 0 print the number and no factors. It is not a general cryptography library and it is not a reason to invent timing claims.

title: false
summary: Exit with a status code indicating failure.
text: Exits with status 1. Bash also has a builtin false. /usr/bin/false --version identifies coreutils. The manual lists false as an ordinary failure status, unlike test's use of 1 as an answer.

title: fmt
summary: Reformat each paragraph in the FILE(s), writing to standard output.
text: Reflows paragraphs to a width. -w sets the width and -p keeps a mail-style prefix. It is not a code formatter and it will join short lines that look like a paragraph. BSD fmt exists with a different option set.

title: fold
summary: Wrap input lines in each FILE, writing to standard output.
text: Wraps lines at a width. On this UTF-8 locale, fold -w 1 split the two bytes of U+00E9. Do not assume a column width keeps a multibyte character intact; check with od. -b counts bytes. -s breaks at spaces.

title: groups
summary: Print group memberships for each USERNAME or, if no USERNAME is specified, for
text: Prints the groups of a user. With no operand it describes the current process. It reads the account database, not the file mode bits. id -Gn is the related coreutils form.

title: head
summary: Print the first 10 lines of each FILE to standard output.
text: Prints a prefix. GNU head -n -5 prints all but the last five lines; BSD head rejects a negative count. -c counts bytes. -z uses NUL as the line delimiter. It does not follow a growing file; tail -f does.

title: hostid
summary: Print the numeric identifier (in hexadecimal) for the current host.
text: Prints a hexadecimal identifier, historically derived from an address. It is not a UUID and not a secret you should publish as an authenticator. Treat the captured value as a fact about this machine only.

title: id
summary: Print user and group information for each specified USER,
text: Prints uid, gid, and groups. -u and -g print numbers. -Z asks for an SELinux context and fails on this kernel. Scripts that parse the default sentence are brittle; use the numeric options.

title: install
summary: This install program copies files (often just compiled) into destination
text: Copies a file and sets its mode, creating parent directories with -D. -C skips the write when the content already matches, which keeps the destination mtime. BSD install uses a different flag set. It is the right tool for placing a built binary into a prefix.

title: join
summary: For each pair of input lines with identical join fields, write a line to
text: Joins two files on a shared field. Both inputs must be sorted on that field. The default GNU check exits 1 on disorder but can still emit a partial line. --nocheck-order returns 0 and can silently drop rows.

title: link
summary: Call the link function to create a link named FILE2 to an existing FILE1.
text: Creates a hard link with link(2) and no extra flags. It will not replace an existing name and it will not link a directory for an unprivileged user. ln is the tool with -s, -f, and -r. unlink is the matching removal call.

title: ln
summary: In the 1st form, create a link to TARGET with the name LINK_NAME.
text: Makes hard and symbolic links. -s is a symlink. GNU -r / --relative rewrites the target as a relative path. -sfn retargets a symlink even when the destination name exists. BSD ln has no --relative.

title: logname
summary: Print the user's login name.
text: Prints the name from the login utmp record. In this non-login sandbox it fails. whoami reads the effective uid instead and still works. Do not use logname as a synonym for the account that owns the files.

title: ls
summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
text: Lists names and, with -l, metadata. The shell expands globs before ls sees them. --quoting-style=shell-escape makes odd names visible. --zero delimits with NUL. GNU -T is tab size; BSD ls -T is a time format. dir and vdir are related entry points.

title: md5sum
summary: Print or check MD5 (128-bit) checksums.
text: MD5 checksums in the GNU text/binary line format. Fine for accidental corruption checks in old manifests. Not a collision-resistant choice for new ones. --check and --status match the other *sum tools. md5sum.textutils is a symlink, not a second algorithm.

title: mkdir
summary: Create the DIRECTORY(ies), if they do not already exist.
text: Creates directories. -p creates parents and does not fail if the leaf exists. -m applies to the final component created in that invocation; parents are created under the current umask, which is 0022 here, so they land at 755 when -m 700 is asked.

title: mkfifo
summary: Create named pipes (FIFOs) with the given NAMEs.
text: Creates a named pipe. Opening it blocks until the other end is opened. A lesson that reads a fifo must bound the wait with timeout, or the sandbox hangs. mkfifo does not copy bytes; the readers and writers do.

title: mknod
summary: Create the special file NAME of the given TYPE.
text: Creates fifos, and device nodes when you pass a type and numbers. Device nodes need privileges this course does not use. Prefer mkfifo for a named pipe. Do not run mknod against /dev in examples.

title: mktemp
summary: Create a temporary file or directory, safely, and print its name.
text: Creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name. The template must end in at least six X characters. -d makes a directory. --suffix appends a suffix after the X's. Leaving the default /tmp is fine; the course scripts also set TMPDIR to the sandbox.

title: mv
summary: Rename SOURCE to DEST, or move SOURCE(s) to DIRECTORY.
text: Renames, or copies and unlinks when the destination is another filesystem. -n refuses to overwrite and, on this GNU version, exits 1. -t collects sources into a directory. There is no cross-device rename system call; EXDEV is why the copy happens.

title: nice
summary: Run COMMAND with an adjusted niceness, which affects process scheduling.
text: Adjusts niceness and runs a command. The manual says a negative adjustment without privilege prints a warning and continues as if the adjustment were zero. The exit status is the command's status, not the warning. renice is a different program and is not coreutils.

title: nl
summary: Write each FILE to standard output, with line numbers added.
text: Numbers lines. -ba is -b a, which numbers every line including blanks. The default body style skips blanks. It is a formatter, not a way to address lines for editing. BSD nl differs in style names.

title: nohup
summary: Run COMMAND, ignoring hangup signals.
text: Runs a command immune to SIGHUP and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects it to nohup.out. When stdout is already redirected, nohup.out is not created. It does not daemonize, and it does not change niceness.

title: nproc
summary: Print the number of processing units available to the current process,
text: Prints the number of processing units available to the process, which can be less than --all when the affinity mask is smaller. --ignore subtracts from that count. GNU documents the default sort --parallel cap in terms of available processors. nproc is not in BSD base.

title: numfmt
summary: Reformat NUMBER(s), or the numbers from standard input if none are specified.
text: Formats numbers with SI or IEC suffixes. 2048 becomes 2.0K in IEC (1024) and 2.1K in SI (1000) because of rounding. --field selects a column. It is GNU-only. It does not change sort's numeric comparison; sort -h has its own rules.

title: od
summary: Write an unambiguous representation, octal bytes by default,
text: Dumps bytes in hex, octal, or named characters. Use it when cat -A is not enough, especially for NULs and encoding mistakes. -An drops the address. -w sets the width. hexdump is a different program and is not coreutils.

title: paste
summary: Write lines consisting of the sequentially corresponding lines from
text: Merges lines from files, or, with -s, joins lines of one file. -d sets the delimiter. -z uses NUL as the record separator. It does not sort or match keys; join does that.

title: pathchk
summary: Diagnose invalid or non-portable file names.
text: Checks whether a name is portable. -p applies the POSIX portable character set and a length limit. A name containing | fails -p. It does not create the file and it does not tell you whether the directory is writable.

title: pinky
summary: in short format
text: A lightweight who. With nobody recorded in utmp it prints a header and no rows, which is what this sandbox shows. It is GNU-specific. who reads the same kind of login records.

title: pr
summary: Paginate or columnate FILE(s) for printing.
text: Paginates and columns text. -t drops the header and footer so the output can go to another filter. -s sets a column separator. It is not a table join. Default headers include the date, so scripts that need stable bytes pass -t.

title: printenv
summary: Print the values of the specified environment VARIABLE(s).
text: Prints the environment or one variable. A missing name exits non-zero, which the manual calls out. -0 uses NUL delimiters. env runs a command; printenv only displays.

title: printf
summary: Print ARGUMENT(s) according to FORMAT, or execute according to OPTION:
text: Formats operands. Bash also has a builtin printf. Use /usr/bin/printf when you need the coreutils binary, including %q for shell quoting. The format string is not a filename. Prefer printf over echo for escapes and missing newlines.

title: ptx
summary: Output a permuted index, including context, of the words in the input files.
text: Builds a permuted index. It is a specialized text tool, not a sort replacement. The output columns are easy to misread; the manual's ptx section documents the format. Most developer workflows never need it.

title: pwd
summary: Print the full filename of the current working directory.
text: Prints the working directory. Bash's builtin pwd is what you get if you type pwd. /usr/bin/pwd is coreutils. -P resolves symlinks; -L follows the logical $PWD. The builtin and the binary agree on this sandbox because the directory is not reached through a link.

title: readlink
summary: Print value of a symbolic link or canonical file name
text: Prints the target of a symlink, or, with -f, a canonical path. -f allows the final component to be missing and still exits 0. -e requires every component to exist. GNU -f is not what older BSD readlink implemented.

title: realpath
summary: Print the resolved absolute file name;
text: Prints an absolute path. The default allows a missing final component. -e requires the path to exist. -m allows missing middle components. --relative-to prints a path relative to a base. Older macOS installs did not ship realpath.

title: rm
summary: Remove (unlink) the FILE(s).
text: Removes directory entries. GNU defaults include --preserve-root. -I prompts once before removing more than three items or descending recursively; an EOF answer left the files in place and still exited 0 in this sandbox. -i prompts per file. It does not shred data.

title: rmdir
summary: Remove the DIRECTORY(ies), if they are empty.
text: Removes empty directories. A non-empty directory and a regular file both fail, with different messages. -p removes parent components if they become empty. Use rm -r only when you mean to delete contents.

title: runcon
summary: Run a program in a different SELinux security context.
text: Runs a command in a different SELinux context. It needs a kernel with SELinux. This host does not have one. It is not a substitute for sudo and not a coreutils permission bit.

title: seq
summary: Print numbers from FIRST to LAST, in steps of INCREMENT.
text: Prints a sequence of numbers. -w equalizes width and -s sets the separator. The floating-point section of the manual applies. On 9.4, seq 0 0.1 1 prints 11 values ending at 1.0 for this particular step; that is not a proof that every step is exact.

title: sha1sum
summary: Print or check SHA1 (160-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-1 checksums, 160-bit, same interface as sha256sum. Collision attacks against SHA-1 are practical. Do not choose it for a new manifest. The manual groups it with the SHA-2 tools even though SHA-1 is not SHA-2.

title: sha224sum
summary: Print or check SHA224 (224-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-224, a truncated SHA-256 variant with a different initial state. Same -c interface. Rare in download pages. Prefer sha256sum unless a protocol names SHA-224.

title: sha256sum
summary: Print or check SHA256 (256-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-256 checksums. This is the usual coreutils tool for a download manifest. --check reads the GNU line format. A wrong hash prints FAILED and exits 1. The digest of the three bytes abc is a known test vector used in the lesson.

title: sha384sum
summary: Print or check SHA384 (384-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-384, the truncated SHA-512 variant. Same command-line shape as sha256sum. Choose it when a protocol says SHA-384, not because the name looks longer than SHA-256.

title: sha512sum
summary: Print or check SHA512 (512-bit) checksums.
text: SHA-512. The digest is longer and the implementation processes 64-bit words. On a small file the runtime difference may sit inside the noise. Use the benchmark if you need a number, and do not generalize it.

title: shred
summary: Overwrite the specified FILE(s) repeatedly, in order to make it harder
text: Overwrites a file, and -u unlinks it afterward. The manual's assumption is that the filesystem and the device overwrite in place. Journals, snapshots, compression, RAID, and SSD wear leveling break that assumption. One pass in a lesson only shows the user interface.

title: shuf
summary: Write a random permutation of the input lines to standard output.
text: Writes a random permutation. There is no --seed. Reproducible draws use --random-source with a file of bytes. -i ranges over integers and -n limits the count. shuf is GNU-only; it is not a sort.

title: sleep
summary: Pause for NUMBER seconds.  SUFFIX may be 's' for seconds (the default),
text: Pauses for a duration. GNU sleep accepts a decimal and the suffixes s, m, h, and d. An invalid interval exits non-zero. It is not a scheduler. timeout is the tool that stops another command.

title: sort
summary: Write sorted concatenation of all FILE(s) to standard output.
text: Orders lines. -s disables the last-resort full-line comparison. -S sets the initial memory buffer (default unit 1024 bytes; M is 1,048,576). -T sets the temporary directory. --parallel defaults to available CPUs capped at 8. Exit status 1 means a -c check failed; 2 means an error.

title: split
summary: Output pieces of FILE to PREFIXaa, PREFIXab, ...;
text: Splits by lines, bytes, or into N chunks. -d uses numeric suffixes. -n r/N round-robins lines, so a file with one line puts everything in the first piece. --filter runs a command per piece. BSD split does not have this -n syntax.

title: stat
summary: Display file or file system status.
text: Prints metadata with a format string. GNU uses -c. BSD uses -f for the format, which is the single most common portability break. stat -f here means filesystem status, and %T can say ext2/ext3 on ext4.

title: stdbuf
summary: Run COMMAND, with modified buffering operations for its standard streams.
text: Adjusts C FILE buffering by preloading libstdbuf.so. The binary contains the strings LD_PRELOAD and libstdbuf.so. cat and dd do not use FILE streams. tee resets its own buffering. -iL is rejected with status 125. It is ELF-only and GNU-only.

title: stty
summary: Print or change terminal characteristics.
text: Changes or prints terminal settings. This course does not run stty against the session terminal, because a bad mode breaks the terminal. Read the manual before using it in a script. It is not a file-permission tool.

title: sum
summary: Print or check BSD (16-bit) checksums.
text: Historic BSD (-r) and System V (-s) checksums. cksum -a bsd and cksum -a sysv cover the same algorithms. Do not use sum for a new integrity check. The output width and algorithm differ between -r and -s.

title: sync
summary: Synchronize cached writes to persistent storage
text: Asks the kernel to flush cached writes. With no operand it syncs all filesystems the process may sync. -f syncs the filesystems that contain the named files. It does not prove a drive's firmware finished the write.

title: tac
summary: Write each FILE to standard output, last line first.
text: Prints lines in reverse. It is GNU-only; BSD users often use tail -r. -s sets a separator, and the separator stays attached to the record, which makes the reversed bytes look surprising until you inspect them with od.

title: tail
summary: Print the last 10 lines of each FILE to standard output.
text: Prints a suffix, or follows a file with -f. -F follows by name and retries. -n +K starts at line K. GNU negative counts on head are a different feature. Follow mode runs until it is killed; bound it with timeout.

title: tee
summary: Copy standard input to each FILE, and also to standard output.
text: Copies stdin to stdout and to files. -a appends. The manual notes that tee adjusts its own buffering, so stdbuf does not control it. It is the coreutils way to save a copy of a pipeline without a shell process substitution.

title: test
summary: Exit with the status determined by EXPRESSION.
text: Evaluates an expression and exits 0 or 1. Bash's builtin test shadows /usr/bin/test. -s is true only for a non-empty file. The manual lists test among the commands whose 0 and 1 are answers. Use spaces around operators.

title: timeout
summary: Start COMMAND, and kill it if still running after DURATION.
text: Runs a command and sends it a signal when the duration elapses. The default exit status is 124 if the command was signaled. --preserve-status returns 128 plus the signal, 143 for SIGTERM. It is GNU-only. macOS users install gtimeout.

title: touch
summary: Update the access and modification times of each FILE to the current time.
text: Updates timestamps or creates an empty file. -d takes a date string and -r copies a timestamp from another file. -c does not create. BSD touch uses -t for a timestamp and does not accept GNU -d.

title: tr
summary: Translate, squeeze, and/or delete characters from standard input,
text: Translates or deletes bytes from stdin. It has no file operands. Character classes such as [:upper:] are locale-sensitive. A UTF-8 character is more than one byte, and tr will rewrite each byte that appears in the set. It is not sed.

title: true
summary: Exit with a status code indicating success.
text: Exits with status 0. The shell builtin is what an unadorned true usually runs. /usr/bin/true --version prints the coreutils banner. Useful as the command argument to nice or timeout when you need a known status.

title: truncate
summary: Shrink or extend the size of each FILE to the specified size
text: Sets a file to a size. Extending a file creates a hole when the filesystem allows it, which is why du and stat then disagree. Shrinking discards the tail from the directory entry's point of view. It is GNU; it is not dd.

title: tsort
summary: Write totally ordered list consistent with the partial ordering in FILE.
text: Topological order of a list of pairs. Input is one pair per line. A cycle makes it fail. It is the coreutils tool for a dependency order, not a general sort, and the input is not a Makefile.

title: tty
summary: Print the file name of the terminal connected to standard input.
text: Prints the terminal name connected to stdin, or fails when stdin is not a terminal. Pipelines and this capture environment are not terminals, so tty exits non-zero. The manual lists tty among special exit statuses.

title: uname
summary: Print certain system information.  With no OPTION, same as -s.
text: Prints kernel and machine facts. -srm is enough to identify the capture class without a hostname. -a includes the nodename. It does not print the coreutils version; ls --version does that.

title: unexpand
summary: Convert blanks in each FILE to tabs, writing to standard output.
text: Turns runs of spaces into tabs. -a converts all runs, not only leading ones. -t must match the tab stops expand used, or the round trip changes columns. It is byte-oriented.

title: uniq
summary: Filter adjacent matching lines from INPUT (or standard input),
text: Collapses adjacent matching lines. It does not search the whole file; sort first. -c counts, -d prints duplicates, -u prints uniques. -i folds case. GNU -z matches sort -z. sort -u is not the same once keys are involved.

title: unlink
summary: Call the unlink function to remove the specified FILE.
text: Removes one name with unlink(2). It does not remove directories. It does not take -r. If another hard link remains, the data remains. rm is the tool with prompts and recursion.

title: users
summary: Output who is currently logged in according to FILE.
text: Prints login names from utmp. This sandbox has no logged-in users, so the output is empty and the status is still 0. An empty line is not an error. who shows the same records with more columns.

title: vdir
summary: List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
text: vdir is ls -l under another name, from the same package. Use it only when you want that default. Scripts should call ls -l so the format is explicit on systems where vdir is absent.

title: wc
summary: Print newline, word, and byte counts for each FILE, and a total line if
text: Counts newlines, words, characters, bytes, and the longest line. -l counts newline bytes, so a file with no trailing newline can have a last line that -l does not count. --files0-from reads NUL-separated names. --total controls the total line.

title: who
summary: Print information about users who are currently logged in.
text: Prints utmp records. With no logins it prints nothing and exits 0. It is coreutils on this Ubuntu. uptime is not, even though people mention them together. Do not parse who to authorize a user.

title: whoami
summary: Print the user name associated with the current effective user ID.
text: Prints the effective user name. It still works when logname fails. It does not print the uid; id -u does. It is not a security boundary.

title: yes
summary: Repeatedly output a line with all specified STRING(s), or 'y'.
text: Repeats a string until the pipe closes. The usual close is SIGPIPE. With pipefail the pipeline can exit 141. Without pipefail the status is the reader's status. Bound it with head. It is not a load generator you should leave running.

title: grep
summary: Line search. Not coreutils. Ubuntu package grep, upstream GNU grep.
text: grep GNU grep grep Line search. Not coreutils. Ubuntu package grep, upstream GNU grep. not coreutils

title: sed
summary: Stream editor. Not coreutils. Ubuntu package sed, upstream GNU sed. sed -i rewrites a file.
text: sed GNU sed sed Stream editor. Not coreutils. Ubuntu package sed, upstream GNU sed. sed -i rewrites a file. not coreutils

title: awk
summary: Not coreutils. On this host /usr/bin/awk resolves to mawk. Installing gawk normally steals the alternative; this host was set back to mawk.
text: awk mawk (Ubuntu default awk) mawk Not coreutils. On this host /usr/bin/awk resolves to mawk. Installing gawk normally steals the alternative; this host was set back to mawk. not coreutils

summary: Not coreutils. Ubuntu package gawk, upstream GNU awk. Call it by path. gensub is not in mawk.

summary: Not coreutils. Directory walk. -print0 is the NUL producer.
text: find GNU findutils findutils Not coreutils. Directory walk. -print0 is the NUL producer. not coreutils
